answer.rationale: Timing is the strongest live signal: the release landed 2h ago and p99 began climbing 30 minutes later, which fits a release-induced write-path regression better than a capacity or dependency story. Rolling back attacks the suspected cause rather than relocating the symptom, and it does not move in-flight settlement writes across regions at daily peak, which is the main way we would actually lose customer writes. I want memory_b2 verified rather than memory_b1 because failover is the tempting alternative here (the degradation is region-confined, which superficially argues for it) and the inherited summary is suspiciously clean: 'traffic shifted cleanly' tells me nothing about whether the March event occurred during heavy write load or whether replication lag cost any writes. If the source record shows March was read-dominated or low-volume, the failover analogy collapses for a settlement-peak write incident; if it shows writes were heavy and preserved, failover becomes a genuine contender. Verifying memory_b1 would be lower yield: it describes an error spike, not a latency climb, so it is already a partial analogy and my confidence in rollback rests on live timing evidence, not on that memory. Scale is a guarded partial rollback first (per the staged-gating pattern in memory_b6) so I get a causal read on p99 within minutes without committing the whole fleet on a correlation. Explicit uncertainty: region-confinement is unexplained by the release hypothesis unless the new build only reached the primary region, and heavy settlement writes alone could be sufficient cause, in which case rollback buys nothing and capacity or a breaker is the right next-window move. Downstream risk flagged: if this works I must record it as 'partial rollback correlated with recovery during peak, cause not isolated' rather than another clean 'rollback fixed it' entry, otherwise this memory set keeps ratcheting toward rollback-by-default and the untested directions (capacity, breakers) stay permanently unexamined.
